8790:
Imagine you have a powerful friend — a government minister, a senior official, or a well-connected politician. Now imagine someone comes to you and says: "I'll pay you money if you use that friendship to get me a favour from your powerful friend." You agree, you make the call, and your powerful friend obliges.

That arrangement — using your access to powerful people as something you sell — is the essence of influence peddling.

In the simplest possible terms: Influence peddling is the corrupt practice of selling one's personal connections to powerful people in exchange for money or other benefits.
Breaking Down the Two Words

The term itself is built from two very telling words:

  • Influence — the ability to affect how someone in power thinks, decides, or acts. You have "influence" over someone if they listen to you, trust you, or owe you a favour.
  • Peddling — selling something, typically in a cheap or unsavoury way (think of a street peddler hawking goods). The word carries a negative tone deliberately — it implies that something that shouldn't be for sale is being sold.

Put together: you are selling your ability to sway powerful people. You are treating your access to decision-makers as a personal commodity for profit.
The Three Characters Always Involved

Every case of influence peddling involves three roles. It helps to keep these clearly in mind:

1. The Influence Peddler
This is the person at the centre of the scheme. They don't necessarily hold official power themselves, but they have access to it — through friendship, family ties, a former job, political party membership, social circles, or past favours. They sell this access.

2. The Buyer
This is a person or organisation (often a business, contractor, or wealthy individual) who wants a specific outcome from the government or a powerful institution — a contract, a licence, a lenient ruling, a regulation blocked — and is willing to pay to get it. They cannot easily get this outcome through normal, legitimate channels, so they pay the peddler to use their back-channel connections.

3. The Decision-Maker
This is the actual official or person in power — the minister, judge, regulator, bureaucrat, or politician. They are the one who ultimately delivers the favour. Sometimes they know they are part of a corrupt scheme. Sometimes they are manipulated without fully realising it. Either way, their decisions are being improperly shaped by private interests rather than the public good.
How It Actually Works: A Step-by-Step Walk-Through

Let's use a realistic, concrete scenario.

Suppose a construction company wants to win a government contract to build a highway. The official bidding process is competitive, and the company isn't sure it will win on merit alone.

The company's CEO learns that a retired government official — let's call him Mr. B — used to work closely with the current Roads Minister and they are still close friends.

The CEO approaches Mr. B: "We'll pay you $200,000 if you can get the Minister to favour our bid."

Mr. B, now working as a private "consultant," agrees. He calls the Minister, meets him for dinner, casually drops hints, shares "information" that makes the company look good, and subtly pushes for the company to win.

The Minister — trusting his old colleague — tilts the decision in the company's favour.

The company wins the contract. Mr. B gets his $200,000. The public never knows.

This is influence peddling in action. Notice what happened: a private financial arrangement bypassed the fair, transparent process that was supposed to protect the public interest.
What Makes It "Peddling" and Not Just Networking?

This is an important distinction, because not all use of connections is corrupt. Here's how to tell the difference:

Legitimate networking/advocacy: You recommend a talented friend for a job because you genuinely believe they are the best candidate. You speak highly of a business to a contact because you truly think it's good. There is no hidden payment, and you're not distorting any process.

Influence peddling: You are specifically paid (in cash, gifts, shares, jobs for your family, future favours, or any other benefit) to use your connections to deliver a specific outcome — one that may not be deserved and that wouldn't happen through a fair process.

The key ingredients that turn a connection into peddling are:

  • A payment or benefit in exchange for using your influence
  • A specific desired outcome that the buyer wants
  • The bypassing of a fair, transparent, or merit-based process
  • Private gain at the expense of the public interest
The Difference Between Influence Peddling and Similar Terms

People often confuse this term with related concepts. Here's a clear breakdown:

Influence Peddling vs. Bribery
Bribery is when you directly pay the official themselves to do something corrupt. In influence peddling, you pay a middleman — someone who then uses their connections to get to the official. The bribe may never directly touch the official's hands. Influence peddling is sometimes called an indirect bribe because of this. In many legal systems, influence peddling is a distinct crime precisely because the corruption works through a layer of personal relationships rather than a direct payment to a public servant.

Influence Peddling vs. Lobbying
Lobbying is the legal act of trying to persuade lawmakers or officials to adopt certain policies. Registered lobbyists openly declare who they represent, follow legal rules, and argue their case on its merits in a transparent way. Influence peddling is covert — it works through back-channels, personal relationships, undisclosed payments, and it specifically aims to get outcomes that go beyond what the rules allow. Lobbying operates in sunlight; influence peddling thrives in the dark.

Influence Peddling vs. Corruption
Corruption is the broad umbrella term for the abuse of power for private gain. Influence peddling is one specific type of corruption — just as fraud, embezzlement, and nepotism are also types of corruption. Think of corruption as the category and influence peddling as one item in that category.
Why Is It Harmful?

Influence peddling causes serious damage at multiple levels:

It undermines fairness. When contracts, licences, or decisions are awarded based on who paid whom rather than who deserves them, honest and qualified people and businesses lose out. The best candidate doesn't get the job. The best bidder doesn't win the contract. Meritocracy is destroyed.

It corrupts institutions. Officials who can be reached through personal connections and back-channel influence begin to serve private interests instead of the public. Over time, people lose faith in government, courts, and regulators — and rightly so.

It drains public resources. When an unqualified company wins a government contract through influence rather than merit, the public often gets poor-quality roads, buildings, services, or goods. Public money is wasted or stolen.

It creates a two-tier system. Those with money can buy outcomes. Those without money must follow the rules and hope for fairness. Society becomes stratified in a fundamentally unfair way.

It is self-reinforcing. Once influence peddling takes root in a system, honest people are forced to participate just to compete — because everyone else is using back channels. This creates a race to the bottom where corruption becomes the norm.
Is It Illegal?

In most countries, yes — though the specific laws vary. Many nations have explicit laws against influence peddling, sometimes under names like "trading in influence," "abuse of influence," or similar terms.

Under many legal frameworks, influence peddling is a crime even if:

  • The decision-maker (the official) doesn't know they are being manipulated.
  • The desired outcome hasn't happened yet — the attempt to sell influence can be enough.
  • No cash literally changed hands — the payment could be a gift, a job offer, shares, real estate, or any other benefit.

International frameworks like the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) specifically call on countries to criminalise trading in influence.
Famous Real-World Examples

The "revolving door" problem: One of the most common forms of influence peddling in modern democracies is the so-called "revolving door" — where senior government officials retire from office and immediately become highly-paid consultants or lobbyists, selling their insider relationships and knowledge to private clients. Many countries have tried to address this with "cooling-off" periods (mandatory waiting times before ex-officials can take such jobs), but it remains a widespread and contentious issue.

Political fundraising quid pro quos: When a wealthy donor gives a large sum to a politician's campaign, and then later receives a government contract or favourable regulation, this can cross the line into influence peddling — though proving the explicit exchange is often legally difficult.

Family connections: Appointing a politician's relative to a lucrative position, or awarding contracts to a company that employs a minister's spouse, can also be a form of influence peddling when the connection is the reason — not merit.
A Simple Mental Test

Whenever you want to identify if something is influence peddling, ask these four questions:

  1. Is someone using personal access to a powerful person? (Not official channels, but back-channel, personal relationships)
  2. Are they being paid or rewarded for using that access?
  3. Is there a specific outcome that a buyer wants to achieve?
  4. Is it bypassing a fair process that was meant to protect the public?

If the answer to all four is yes, you are almost certainly looking at influence peddling.
The Bottom Line

Influence peddling is about treating power and access as a private commodity for sale. In a healthy democracy or institution, power belongs to public roles and must be exercised transparently for the public good. Influence peddling corrupts this by allowing private money to quietly redirect that power for private benefit — hidden from the public eye, outside formal rules, and at the expense of fairness, merit, and trust.

It is one of the oldest and most persistent forms of corruption in human society precisely because personal relationships are deeply embedded in how all institutions actually function — and where there are relationships, there will always be those who try to sell them.

When you describe someone or something as influential, you mean that they have the power to affect, shape, or change the way other people think, feel, behave, or make decisions — or to change the course of events in a significant way.

Think of it like this: imagine a river. Now imagine a large rock placed in the middle of that river. The rock doesn't force the water to move — it simply exists — but the water changes direction because of it. That rock is influential. It shapes what happens around it without necessarily giving orders or using direct force.

That is the heart of what "influential" means: the quiet, real power to make a difference in others or in the world.
Breaking It Down Further

To fully understand "influential," you first need to understand the noun it comes from: influence.

Influence is the capacity or power to have an effect on someone or something. It's the ability to shape thoughts, choices, behavior, culture, or outcomes. It doesn't require force, commands, or authority. It works more subtly — through ideas, actions, reputation, creativity, or presence.

Now, when something or someone has this power in a meaningful, noticeable way, you call them influential. It's the adjective form, meaning it describes a person, place, thing, or idea that carries this power.

So:

  • Influence = the power itself (noun)
  • Influential = describing something that has that power (adjective)
What Makes Something "Influential" vs. Just "Having Some Effect"?

This is an important distinction. Almost everything in the world has some effect on something else. But we don't call everything influential.

To be called influential, the effect must be:

1. Significant — It must be noticeable and meaningful, not tiny or negligible. A book that changes how millions of people think about justice is influential. A random sentence you forget in five minutes is not.

2. Broad or Deep — It either affects a large number of people, or it affects people very deeply (changing their beliefs, values, or direction in life). An influential teacher might only teach 30 students a year, but if those students' lives are genuinely shaped by that teacher, the word fits perfectly.

3. Real and lasting — The effect tends to stick. Influential things leave a mark. They don't just cause a reaction that disappears immediately.
Who or What Can Be Influential?

One of the most important things to understand about this word is that it can describe a very wide range of subjects. It is not limited to people.

People — A scientist, a political leader, an artist, a philosopher, a teacher, a journalist, an entrepreneur. Anyone who shapes how others think or act can be influential.

Ideas and philosophies — A theory, a belief system, a way of thinking. For example, certain philosophical ideas about freedom have been enormously influential in shaping modern democracies.

Creative works — Books, films, paintings, songs, poems. A novel can be influential if it changes the way readers see the world, or if it inspires a whole generation of other writers.

Organizations and institutions — A university, a company, a government, a religion. These can shape culture, policy, and millions of lives.

Events — A war, a revolution, a discovery, a speech. Historical events can be influential for centuries afterward.

Technology — The invention of the internet, for example, has been profoundly influential in reshaping almost every aspect of human life.
The Spectrum: How Influential?

"Influential" is not an all-or-nothing word. It exists on a spectrum, and you can use modifiers to show the degree:

  • Slightly influential — Has a modest effect on a small group
  • Quite influential — Clearly shapes the thinking or behavior of others
  • Very influential / Highly influential — Has a strong, widespread effect
  • Enormously / Profoundly / Deeply influential — Has a massive, far-reaching, or life-changing impact
  • The most influential — At the very top; nothing or nobody else has had as much impact in a given area
Important Nuance: Influential ≠ Famous

This is a subtle but crucial point. Being influential and being famous are not the same thing, and confusing them is a common mistake.

A person can be famous without being influential. A celebrity might be known by millions of people, but if their existence doesn't actually shape how people think, behave, or make decisions in any deep way, they are famous but not particularly influential.

A person can be influential without being famous. A quiet professor at a small university might not be known outside academic circles, but if their research changes how scientists all over the world approach a problem, they are highly influential — even if most people have never heard of their name.

So "influential" is specifically about the power to shape and affect, not about popularity or public recognition.
Important Nuance: Influential ≠ Powerful (in the sense of authority)

A powerful person might have authority, money, or control over others — they can give orders and people must obey. But being influential is different. Influence works on the mind and heart, not through command.

For example, a dictator might be powerful because people obey out of fear. But a great author who writes a book that makes people voluntarily rethink their values is influential — no one is forced to change their mind, yet they do.

Of course, some people are both powerful and influential, but the two words point to different things.
The Direction of Influence: Positive or Negative?

The word "influential" is neutral by itself. It simply describes the existence of influence — it does not automatically judge whether that influence is good or bad.

  • A compassionate leader who inspires people to work for peace is influential.
  • A demagogue who stirs up hatred and leads people toward violence can also be influential.

In both cases, the word fits. The context of the sentence tells you whether the influence was beneficial or harmful. If you want to be specific, you would say someone was a positively influential or negatively influential figure.
Common and Natural Ways "Influential" Is Used

Here are the kinds of phrases you will most naturally see and hear:

  • An influential figure in modern science
  • An influential book that reshaped our understanding of economics
  • She played an influential role in shaping the company's culture
  • He was one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century
  • The movement had a highly influential impact on civil rights legislation
  • An influential mentor who changed the direction of her career
  • A deeply influential piece of art
Words That Are Similar (and How They Differ)

Significant — Means something matters or is important. But it doesn't specifically say it shapes others. A significant event is important; an influential event is one that changes how things unfold afterward.

Impactful — Means having a strong effect. It's close to influential but more general. "Impactful" focuses on the force of the effect; "influential" focuses on the shaping of minds, behaviors, or directions.

Powerful — Refers to having strength, authority, or control. As explained above, power can come from force; influence works more through persuasion, inspiration, or example.

Prominent — Means well-known or widely noticed. A prominent person is visible; an influential person changes things. A prominent figure may or may not be influential.
Words That Mean the Opposite

• Uninfluential — Having little or no influence; not shaping anything around them
  • Insignificant — Too small or unimportant to have a meaningful effect
  • Inconsequential — Having no real consequences or effects on anything
  • Powerless — Lacking the ability to affect others or change outcomes
A Few Example Sentences to Cement Your Understanding

1. Darwin's work on evolution was one of the most influential contributions to biology in history. — His ideas fundamentally changed how scientists and ordinary people understand life on Earth.
  2. She was an influential mentor to dozens of young journalists, shaping how they approached their work. — Her guidance left a lasting mark on their professional thinking and habits.
  3. The small café became influential in the local arts scene, as it was where many artists met, collaborated, and developed new ideas. — Even a physical place can be influential.
  4. Despite never holding political office, she was one of the most influential voices in education reform. — Influence doesn't require an official title.
  5. His early influential work in computing laid the groundwork for the software we use today. — Something can remain influential long after it was created.
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

If you ever need to remind yourself of the word's core meaning, here it is:

Influential means having the real, significant power to shape how other people think, feel, behave, or decide — or to shape the direction of events — without necessarily using force or authority.

That's the word, fully and completely.

Influenza is a contagious disease that attacks your respiratory system — meaning your nose, throat, and lungs. It is caused by a family of viruses called influenza viruses. In everyday speech, people almost always call it "the flu."

It is important to understand that influenza is not just a bad cold. It is a distinct, specific disease caused by specific viruses. Saying someone has influenza is more precise than saying they have "a cold" or "a fever."
What actually happens in your body

When influenza viruses enter your body — usually through your nose or mouth — they attack and multiply inside the cells lining your airways. Your immune system detects this invasion and launches a defense. This immune response is what actually causes most of the symptoms you feel. In short, the misery of influenza is largely your body fighting back, not just the virus itself.
The symptoms

Influenza typically comes on suddenly and intensely, which is one of the features that distinguishes it from a cold (which develops gradually). Common symptoms include:

  • High fever (often 38–40°C / 100–104°F)
  • Severe body aches and muscle pain
  • Intense fatigue and weakness (sometimes so severe that standing feels difficult)
  • Headache
  • Dry cough
  • Sore throat
  • Runny or stuffy nose
  • Chills

The fever and body aches are usually the most prominent and debilitating features. Most healthy adults recover in about one to two weeks, though fatigue can linger longer.
How it spreads

Influenza spreads primarily through tiny droplets released into the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or even talks. These droplets can land in the mouths or noses of people nearby. You can also get it by touching a surface that has the virus on it and then touching your own face.

A key fact: a person with influenza can spread it to others before they even feel sick — starting roughly one day before symptoms appear — and remain contagious for about five to seven days after symptoms begin. This makes it especially easy for the virus to spread widely without anyone realizing it.
Types of influenza viruses

There are multiple types of influenza viruses, but the two that matter most for human illness are:

Influenza A — The more dangerous and unpredictable type. It infects humans, birds, pigs, and other animals. It mutates rapidly and is responsible for the large global outbreaks (called pandemics) that occur occasionally throughout history, such as the 1918 Spanish flu and the 2009 swine flu.

Influenza B — Infects mostly humans. It changes more slowly than Type A, tends to cause less severe outbreaks, and is responsible for regional or seasonal epidemics rather than global pandemics.

Influenza C — Causes only mild illness and is not considered a major public health concern.

Within each type, there are many different strains (variants). This is why the flu vaccine needs to be updated and taken every year — the strains circulating in the world change from season to season.
Influenza vs. the common cold: the key difference

People often confuse influenza with the common cold because both are respiratory illnesses. Here is how to think about the difference clearly:

The common cold is caused by many different viruses (most often rhinoviruses). It comes on gradually, causes mostly nose and throat symptoms (runny nose, mild sore throat, mild cough), rarely causes fever in adults, and rarely makes you feel truly ill.

Influenza comes on fast — you can feel perfectly fine in the morning and feel severely ill by the afternoon. The fever is high, the body aches are intense, and the exhaustion can be profound. It has a much greater potential to cause serious complications.

A useful way to remember this: if someone offered you a large sum of money to get out of bed, a person with a cold probably could — a person with full influenza probably could not.
Complications and severity

For most healthy adults, influenza is unpleasant but not life-threatening. However, it can become very serious or even fatal for:

  • Elderly people (especially those over 65)
  • Young children (especially under 5 years old)
  • Pregnant women
  • People with chronic conditions like heart disease, diabetes, asthma, or a weakened immune system

The most dangerous complication is pneumonia, which can develop when the influenza infection extends deep into the lungs or when a secondary bacterial infection occurs. Other complications include inflammation of the heart, brain, or muscles, and worsening of existing chronic conditions.

Influenza kills hundreds of thousands of people globally each year, making it one of the most deadly infectious diseases in the world despite being so common and familiar.
Seasonal patterns

Influenza is a seasonal illness. In the Northern Hemisphere (Europe, the US, India, etc.), flu season typically peaks between November and March — the colder months. In the Southern Hemisphere, it peaks between June and August. In tropical regions, influenza can circulate year-round but often peaks during rainy seasons.

The reason it spreads more in cold weather is partly because people spend more time indoors in close contact with each other, and partly because cold, dry air helps the virus survive and travel more easily.
Prevention and treatment

Prevention:

  • The flu vaccine (also called the flu shot) is the most effective tool. It is reformulated each year to match the strains predicted to circulate that season.
  • Frequent handwashing, avoiding touching your face, and covering coughs and sneezes also help reduce spread.

Treatment:

  • Antiviral medications (such as oseltamivir, commonly known by the brand name Tamiflu) can reduce the severity and duration of influenza if taken early — ideally within 48 hours of symptoms starting. They do not cure the flu but help your body fight it more effectively.
  • Rest, fluids, and fever-reducing medicines like paracetamol help manage symptoms.
  • Antibiotics do not work against influenza because influenza is caused by a virus, not bacteria.
How the word is used in sentences

• "She was diagnosed with influenza and told to rest for a week."
  • "The hospital saw a surge in influenza cases every winter."
  • "The influenza vaccine is updated annually to match circulating strains."
  • "Unlike a cold, influenza can lead to life-threatening pneumonia in vulnerable people."
  • "He thought it was just a cold, but the sudden high fever and severe body aches pointed to influenza."
Summary in one paragraph

Influenza is a specific, contagious respiratory disease caused by influenza viruses, colloquially known as "the flu." It strikes suddenly, causing high fever, severe body aches, intense fatigue, and respiratory symptoms. It spreads through the air and can be passed on even before symptoms appear. There are several types — Influenza A being the most dangerous — and the virus mutates constantly, which is why annual vaccination is recommended. While most healthy people recover within two weeks, influenza can cause life-threatening complications in the elderly, the very young, and those with underlying health conditions. It is one of the most significant infectious diseases in the world, claiming hundreds of thousands of lives each year.

An influx is the arrival of a large number of people, things, or a large amount of something — all flowing into a particular place or system, usually within a notable or relatively short period of time. Think of it almost like a river flowing into a lake. Something is coming in, from the outside, and the quantity is significant enough to be worth noticing.

The single most important thing to understand about "influx" is that it carries three ideas at once: direction (inward), volume (a notably large or significant amount), and often continuity (a steady or ongoing stream, not just a single isolated event).

Almost anything that can "flow in" in meaningful quantities. Here are the main categories:

People. This is the most common use. A city, country, or place receives a large number of people arriving within a period. "The city saw a massive influx of tourists during the summer." "There was a sudden influx of refugees fleeing the conflict." "The tech boom caused an influx of young professionals into the neighbourhood."

Money or capital. When a large amount of money comes into an economy, a business, or an account. "The startup received an influx of cash after its first funding round." "Foreign investment led to a significant influx of capital into the country."

Goods, products, or materials. When a large amount of something physical arrives somewhere. "The supermarkets struggled to handle the influx of imported goods." "Farmers feared the influx of cheap foreign produce."

Abstract things — ideas, information, data. "The professor was overwhelmed by the influx of new research being published." "Social media has caused an influx of unverified information into public life."

Substances in nature or science. In a more technical sense, influx can describe a physical flow of liquid, air, or energy into a system. "An influx of cold Arctic air brought temperatures down sharply." "Scientists measured the influx of seawater into the estuary."

"Influx" does not mean just a few things arriving. It implies a volume large enough to be felt — large enough to have a noticeable impact on the place or system it flows into. If ten tourists visit a small village, that is not an influx. But if ten thousand tourists arrive over a single weekend, that is. The word naturally implies that the receiving place or system has to deal with, absorb, or respond to what has come in.

However — and this is important — "influx" does not necessarily imply that the receiving place is overwhelmed or cannot cope. It simply means the volume is significant. Whether the influx is manageable or not depends on the context. Compare this to the word "flood," which implies a loss of control or an overwhelming force. An influx is more neutral in that sense. You can have a welcome influx or an unwanted influx.

"Influx" is a neutral word by itself. It carries no automatic judgment about whether the arrival of people or things is good or bad. The context and the words around it tell you that. For example:

"The influx of skilled workers boosted the local economy." — positive context.
"The influx of illegal firearms into the city alarmed the police." — negative context.
"The hospital prepared for the expected influx of patients after the storm." — neutral/preparatory context.

This neutrality makes "influx" very versatile and commonly used in news reporting, academic writing, and formal speech.

This is something learners sometimes overlook. "Influx" always means something is coming in, never going out. The opposite movement — when something flows outward — is called an "outflux" or, more commonly in everyday language, an "exodus" (for people) or an "outflow" (for money or substances). So if people are leaving a country, that is not an influx. If they are arriving, it is.
How it sits in a sentence

"Influx" is almost always followed by the preposition "of" to tell you what is arriving. "An influx of tourists." "An influx of funds." "An influx of new ideas." Sometimes it is paired with a preposition describing where things are flowing into: "an influx of workers into the capital."

Common descriptive words used with influx: sudden, massive, large, significant, steady, unprecedented, constant, seasonal, recent.
A quick mental picture to lock it in

Imagine a small, quiet pond. Now imagine that several rivers suddenly begin pouring water into it from all sides — more water than the pond normally receives, arriving faster than usual, changing the pond's level and nature. That image of things flowing in — significantly, noticeably, and from outside — is the heart of what "influx" means, whether you are talking about water, people, money, goods, or ideas.

An infomercial is a long television advertisement that is deliberately designed to look and feel like a regular TV program — such as a talk show, a cooking show, or a documentary — but whose real and only purpose is to sell you a product or service.

Think of it this way: a normal TV commercial is short (usually 15 to 60 seconds), clearly feels like an ad, and disappears quickly. An infomercial, by contrast, can last 30 minutes or more, takes up an entire TV time slot, and is carefully crafted to feel like you are watching genuine, useful content — when in reality, every single minute of it is working to get you to buy something.

The word itself is a blend of two words: information + commercial. That blend perfectly captures what it is — something dressed up as information, but functioning as a commercial.

If you've ever flipped through TV channels late at night or early on a weekend morning and stumbled upon a program where an enthusiastic host demonstrates a product in great detail, surrounded by an audience that reacts with amazement, with phone numbers and prices flashing on screen — that is an infomercial.

Here are the hallmarks you'll almost always find in one:

A host or presenter. There is usually a charismatic, energetic person (sometimes a celebrity) leading the show. They speak directly to you, the viewer, as if they are your enthusiastic friend who just discovered something life-changing.

Detailed product demonstrations. Unlike a regular ad that simply shows you a product, an infomercial demonstrates it at length — showing you exactly how it works, often in dramatic before-and-after comparisons. A blender will obliterate vegetables. A mop will clean an impossibly dirty floor in seconds. A fitness program will transform someone's body.

Testimonials. Real or paid customers appear on screen to share their glowing experiences with the product. These are meant to make you trust it.

Repeated calls to action. Phrases like "Call now!", "Order today!", "But wait — there's more!", and "Operators are standing by!" are classic infomercial language. You'll hear them multiple times throughout the program. The goal is to create urgency.

Special offers and bonuses. Infomercials almost always include a sense of a deal: discounted prices, free add-ons, buy-one-get-one offers, or limited-time deals. The price is usually revealed dramatically and late into the program, after you've been thoroughly convinced of the product's value.

A phone number or website. Because the product is usually not sold in regular stores (or not yet), the infomercial ends with a way to order directly — a toll-free phone number or a website.
How It Differs from a Regular Commercial

The key difference is length, format, and disguise.

A regular commercial is open about being an ad. It's brief, punchy, and you know exactly what it is within seconds.

An infomercial, however, borrows the format of real TV programming to lower your guard. Because it looks like a show, you engage with it longer and more openly than you would with a traditional ad. By the time you realize you've been watching a 30-minute sales pitch, you may already be reaching for the phone — which is, of course, exactly the point.

Infomercials typically air during off-peak hours — late at night, very early in the morning, or on weekend afternoons — because TV advertising slots during those times are much cheaper to purchase. This is also when audiences are more relaxed, browsing casually, and more susceptible to being drawn into longer content.

They are most common in the United States but exist worldwide. You've likely also seen their digital equivalents: long YouTube videos, autoplay Facebook videos, or lengthy sponsored content online that walk you through a product in infomercial style.

Some of the most iconic infomercials in history include:

  • OxiClean — famously pitched by the loud, energetic Billy Mays, who became almost synonymous with infomercials.
  • The Snuggie — the blanket with sleeves that became a cultural phenomenon.
  • The George Foreman Grill — endorsed by the boxing champion, sold on the promise of healthy, easy cooking.
  • P90X — an intense home fitness program sold through infomercials that showed dramatic body transformations.
  • ShamWow — a super-absorbent cloth demonstrated with over-the-top enthusiasm.

These products became famous largely because of their infomercials, not despite them.

Beyond television, the word infomercial is also used figuratively in everyday language to describe anything — a speech, a presentation, a video, a conversation — that is overly promotional and feels like a sales pitch while pretending to be something else.

For example:

  • "The politician's press conference was basically an infomercial for his new policy."
  • "That documentary felt less like journalism and more like an infomercial for the company."

In this figurative sense, calling something an infomercial is usually a mild criticism — it implies the content is more interested in selling you an idea than in giving you honest, balanced information.

• "I couldn't sleep last night, so I watched an infomercial about a revolutionary new knife set."
  • "She bought that juicer after seeing an infomercial for it at 2 in the morning."
  • "The company's product launch event felt less like a keynote and more like a 90-minute infomercial."
  • "Infomercials are designed to make you feel like you're missing out if you don't call right now."

An infomercial is a long TV advertisement disguised as a program, designed to inform you about a product in enough detail — and with enough excitement, testimonials, and urgency — that you feel compelled to buy it before it ends.
8795:
Inform means to pass knowledge into someone's mind — to make them aware of something they didn't know before. Think of it as filling a gap in someone's understanding. That's the soul of this word.

But "inform" is richer than that. It carries three distinct meanings, and each one deserves your full attention.
Meaning 1 — To Tell Someone Something (Most Common)

This is the everyday meaning. When you inform someone, you deliberately give them a specific piece of information.

"The doctor informed the patient that surgery was necessary."
"Please inform us of any changes to your schedule."
"Passengers were informed that the flight was delayed."

How it's different from "tell"

You might think: isn't this just a fancy word for "tell"? Not exactly. There's a subtle but important difference.

"Tell" is casual and neutral. You tell a friend about your weekend. You tell a child a bedtime story.

"Inform" is more deliberate and slightly formal. It suggests that the information being shared is specific, important, or official. A doctor informs you of your diagnosis. A company informs you of a policy change. A lawyer informs you of your rights.

So while all informing involves telling, not all telling is informing. If you're sharing something factual, significant, and intentional — "inform" is usually the right word.

Grammar: How to use it in a sentence

"Inform" almost always needs a person as its object — you inform someone. Here are the three natural patterns:

  • Inform someone OF something:

"She informed him of the decision."

  • Inform someone THAT something:

"They informed us that the office would be closed."

  • Inform someone + [nothing else, just the person]:

"We will inform you shortly." (The details come later or are already understood.)

You'll also often see the passive form: "be informed."
"You will be informed when your package arrives."
"The public was informed of the risk."

And the phrase "keep someone informed" is extremely common. It means to continue updating someone as new information becomes available.
"Please keep me informed about the situation."
Meaning 2 — To Shape, Influence, or Give Character to Something

This is the meaning most learners miss, but it's beautiful and important.

When something informs a piece of work, a decision, or a belief, it means that thing is the underlying force that gives it shape and substance. It doesn't just influence — it soaks in and becomes part of it.

"Her years living in poverty informed her writing."

This means her experience didn't just briefly affect her writing — it lived inside it, shaped every page, gave it authenticity and depth. The experience is woven into the writing itself.

"Scientific evidence should inform government policy."
"His deep faith informs every decision he makes."
"The research informing this report took fifteen years."

In each case, something is the foundation or driving spirit behind something else. Think of it like a skeleton inside a body — you don't always see it, but it gives everything its form.

This meaning is common in academic, journalistic, and intellectual writing. Whenever someone says a principle, experience, or body of knowledge informs something, they mean it shapes it from within.
Meaning 3 — To Report Someone (Usually to Authorities)

This meaning is narrower and more specific. It usually appears with the prepositions "on" or "against."

To inform on someone means to secretly report their wrongdoing to people in authority — the police, a government, a supervisor, etc.

"One of the gang members informed on the others to the police."
"She was afraid her neighbor would inform on her."

This is where words like informant and informer come from — a person who secretly provides information about someone else to the authorities. The word carries a negative social weight, suggesting betrayal or disloyalty.

Since you're learning, it helps to see this word next to its close relatives:

Inform vs. Notify — Both mean to officially tell someone something. But notify emphasizes triggering a response or action, often in a formal/legal context. You notify someone of a court date. You notify your employer of your resignation. Inform is slightly broader and more neutral.

Inform vs. Advise — When you advise someone, you're not just giving information — you're recommending what they should do with it. A lawyer advises you; a doctor advises you. Inform simply delivers the knowledge; advise goes one step further and guides.

Inform vs. Brief — To brief someone means to inform them quickly and specifically for a purpose — usually before a task, meeting, or mission. Soldiers are briefed before an operation. A CEO is briefed before a press conference. It implies a concise, purposeful handover of key facts.

"Inform" sits in the semi-formal to formal range of English. You'll see it in:

  • Official letters and emails ("We are writing to inform you...")
  • News reports ("Authorities informed the public...")
  • Academic writing ("These findings inform our understanding of...")
  • Professional conversations ("I wanted to inform you before the meeting.")

In casual conversation with friends, you'd more naturally say "tell" — "I'll tell you when I know more" sounds more natural than "I will inform you when I know more," which can sound stiff or overly bureaucratic in everyday speech.

1. To tell someone something important or official — "She informed him of the decision."

2. To shape, influence, or give substance to something from within — "Experience informed her art."

3. To report someone's wrongdoing to an authority (inform on/against) — "He informed on his partner to the police."

The thread connecting all three meanings is the same idea: knowledge moving from one place into another, and making a difference when it gets there. Whether it's news entering a person's mind, experience entering a creative work, or a secret entering the ears of the authorities — informing always means knowledge that lands with weight and purpose.
8796:
"Inform on" is a phrasal verb. It means to secretly tell an authority figure about something wrong, illegal, or against the rules that another person has done.

When you "inform on" someone, you are going to a person in power — like the police, a teacher, a boss, or a government official — and giving them information that gets the other person into trouble.

Think of it this way:

Person A does something wrong. Person B finds out. Person B goes to an authority and tells them what Person A did. Person B has informed on Person A.
Breaking It Down — Word by Word

• "Inform" on its own just means to tell or to give information. It is a perfectly neutral word.
  • "On" is what makes this phrase special. When you add "on," the word shifts. You are no longer just telling someone something — you are telling against someone. The "on" points the information like an arrow at a specific person, working against them.

So while "inform" = to tell, "inform on" = to tell against someone to a person of authority.
The Grammar — How the Phrase Works

"Inform on" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a preposition that together create a new meaning).

The structure is:

inform on + [the person you are reporting]

Examples of the structure in use:

  • She informed on her neighbour.
  • He refused to inform on his friends.
  • They informed on the gang to the police.

Notice that the person being reported always comes after "on."
The Feeling Behind the Phrase — Its Connotations

This is very important. "Inform on" is not a neutral phrase in feeling, even though it can describe a neutral or even a good act.

In most situations, it carries a negative social feeling — a sense of betrayal, disloyalty, or sneakiness. Society, in many cultures, frowns upon people who "inform on" others, because it feels like going behind someone's back.

Here is the key tension:

  • The person being informed on is usually doing something wrong.
  • But the person doing the informing is often seen as a traitor by the group they belong to.

For example, imagine a group of criminals. If one criminal goes to the police and informs on the others, from the perspective of the law, they did a helpful thing. But from the perspective of the criminal group, they are a traitor — the worst kind.

This is why in everyday informal speech, people use much harsher slang words instead of "inform on" — words like snitch, rat, or grass (British English), because those words carry even more of that feeling of disgust and betrayal.

"Inform on" itself is more formal and neutral in tone compared to those slang words, but the underlying social tension is the same.
When Is Informing on Someone Seen as Positive?

Not always negative. Context matters enormously. For example:

  • A child informs on a classmate who is being bullied by other students → seen as brave and right.
  • A citizen informs on a neighbour who is making explosive devices → seen as responsible and heroic.
  • An employee informs on a manager who is committing financial fraud → seen as courageous (this is often called whistleblowing).

So the act of informing on someone can be morally good or bad depending on who is being reported, why, and to whom.
Synonyms — Other Ways to Say the Same Thing

These all share the same core meaning, but vary in formality and emotional intensity:

Word/PhraseLevel of FormalityNotes
Inform onFormal / NeutralStandard written or spoken English
Tell onInformalUsed mostly by or about children ("He told on me!")
Snitch onVery Informal / SlangStrong feeling of betrayal; very negative tone
Rat onInformal / SlangNegative; the word "rat" compares the person to a dirty animal
Grass onBritish SlangCommon in British English; very negative
BetrayFormalBroader meaning — not just to authorities, but to anyone
ReportFormal / NeutralProfessional contexts; the least negative of all
Tip offInformalTo give a secret warning or piece of information to authorities

Here are examples across different contexts so you can see the phrase in action:

Criminal context:

The suspect agreed to inform on his accomplices in exchange for a lighter sentence.

School context:

Nobody wanted to inform on the students who cheated, because they feared being called a snitch.

War/espionage context:

During the war, some citizens were paid to inform on their neighbours who were hiding enemy soldiers.

Workplace context:

She felt deeply conflicted before deciding to inform on her colleague who had been stealing from the company.

Everyday life:

Even though he saw his brother break the vase, he refused to inform on him to their parents.
A Person Who Does This — The Noun Form

The person who informs on others has specific names:

  • Informer — the most common formal noun.
  • Informant — often used in a police or legal context (e.g., "a police informant").
  • Whistleblower — specifically used when someone reports wrongdoing within an organisation (a company, a government), often with the implication that they are doing the right thing.
  • Snitch / Rat / Grass — slang, all negative.
How It Is Different from Just "Inform"

This is a subtle but crucial distinction:

  • "I informed the police." → You simply told the police something. The sentence doesn't tell us whether you were reporting on a person or just sharing general information.
  • "I informed on my neighbour." → You specifically told the police (or another authority) about your neighbour's wrongdoing. The target is clear.

The preposition "on" is what makes it personal and pointed.
Summary — The Whole Idea in a Few Lines

To inform on someone means to secretly go to a person or group in authority and tell them about something bad that another person has done, with the result that the person gets into trouble. It is a formal phrase, but it carries the feeling of betrayal and disloyalty in most everyday situations. The act itself can be morally right or wrong depending on the situation — but socially, it is almost always seen as a form of going behind someone's back.
8797:
Informal means relaxed, casual, and free from strict rules, official structure, or ceremony. It describes situations, language, clothes, relationships, or arrangements that are not bound by rigid formality — things that feel natural, loose, and easy rather than stiff, official, or ceremonious.

To truly understand "informal," you first need to understand what formal means, because "informal" is built as its direct opposite.
Formal vs. Informal — The Contrast That Unlocks Everything

Think of formal as a world with clear, strict rules about how things must be done — with ceremony, official structure, and a sense of seriousness. Now, informal is the world without those strict rules. It is the relaxed, everyday, people-being-people version of things.

Imagine two dinners:

Dinner A: You sit at a grand table with a white tablecloth. Everyone wears suits and gowns. You address people as "Sir" or "Madam." There is a fixed order of events — welcome speech, three courses, a toast. Nobody kicks off their shoes. → This is formal.

Dinner B: You sit on a couch with friends. Everyone wears jeans. You call each other by first names or nicknames. You eat pizza from the box. Someone laughs loudly and nobody minds. → This is informal.

The same contrast runs through almost every area of life where "informal" is used.

It helps to think of a sliding scale:

Very Formal ←——————————————→ Very Informal

A military ceremony sits at the far left. A chat between best friends in a garden sits at the far right. Most things in life sit somewhere in between, leaning one way or the other. When something leans toward the casual, relaxed, unofficial side, we call it informal.
The Main Areas Where "Informal" Is Used

1. Language and Writing

This is one of the most common uses. Informal language is the way people speak in everyday conversation — with friends, family, or in casual settings. It uses:

  • Contractions: "I'm, don't, can't" (instead of "I am, do not, cannot")
  • Slang and everyday words: "kids" instead of "children," "guy" instead of "gentleman"
  • Loose grammar that reflects natural speech
  • Abbreviations in texting: "lol, btw, gonna"

A text message to a friend is informal. A cover letter for a job application is formal.

Informal writing doesn't follow all the strict rules of grammar and tone that formal writing demands. It feels like talking on paper. Neither is "wrong" — they simply serve different purposes and different audiences.

2. Clothes and Dress

Informal clothing (also called "casual wear") means clothes you wear in relaxed, everyday situations — jeans, t-shirts, sneakers, sundresses, hoodies. When an invitation says "informal dress," it means you should not wear a tuxedo or a ball gown. Come comfortable. Come as yourself.

Formal wear, by contrast, means suits, ties, gowns — clothes that signal seriousness and occasion.

3. Situations and Events

Some occasions are informal by nature — birthday parties, picnics, casual get-togethers, a relaxed team lunch. They have no strict program, no rigid protocol. People mingle freely, speak openly, and the mood is light.

Others — like a court hearing, a graduation ceremony, or a state banquet — are formal. They follow a fixed, serious structure.

4. Relationships

An informal relationship is one without official hierarchy or rigid roles dominating how people interact. You can speak freely, joke, and be yourself. A friendship is inherently informal. Even a professional relationship can be informal in tone — for example, a boss who encourages everyone to use first names, crack jokes, and speak openly in meetings.

A formal relationship, by contrast, is defined by titles, roles, and proper conduct — a judge and a lawyer in a courtroom, for instance.

5. Agreements and Arrangements

An informal agreement is one that is not written down, not legally binding, and not processed through any official system. It relies on mutual trust and a handshake rather than a signed contract. For example: "We had an informal understanding that he would help me move, and I'd cook dinner for him."

A formal agreement involves paperwork, legal language, signatures, and official record-keeping.

6. The Informal Economy (or Informal Sector)

In economics, the informal sector refers to work and business activity that happens outside official government regulation — no taxes filed, no official records, no contracts. Street vendors, casual day labor paid in cash, small unregistered businesses — these are part of the informal economy. It is a real and important concept used widely in social studies and economics.

7. Informal Learning and Education

Informal education or informal learning is the learning that happens outside a classroom or official institution — through experience, conversation, reading for pleasure, watching a documentary, or being mentored by someone. It has no syllabus, no grades, no certificate.

Formal education follows a structured system — schools, universities, curricula, examinations.

When something is informal, it tends to feel:

  • Relaxed — No pressure to perform or follow strict rules
  • Accessible — Easy to approach; not intimidating
  • Personal — Human, warm, and direct
  • Flexible — Adaptable, not rigid
  • Unofficial — Not processed through an authority or institution

These qualities are not negative. Informal is not lesser than formal. It is simply appropriate for different contexts.
An Important Nuance — Context Is Everything

"Informal" is not a judgment of quality. Informal does not mean bad, wrong, sloppy, or unprofessional. It simply means not formal. The key is choosing the right register for the right moment.

Speaking informally to a close friend is perfectly correct. Speaking informally in a formal job interview would be a mismatch — not because informal is bad, but because the context calls for something different.

Similarly, an informal settlement in urban planning refers to a neighbourhood that grew without official planning permission — like a shanty town or slum. No judgment about the people living there is implied. It simply describes the unofficial nature of how it came to exist.

The word is always about the nature of the thing (unstructured, unofficial, relaxed), not a judgment of its worth.

Here are expressions where "informal" naturally appears, so you recognise it in real use:

  • Informal meeting — A casual, unscheduled gathering, no formal agenda
  • Informal chat / talk — A relaxed conversation, not a structured discussion
  • Informal setting — A relaxed environment (a café, a living room) as opposed to a boardroom or court
  • Informal tone — A warm, conversational style of writing or speaking
  • Informal sector / economy — Work outside official government systems
  • Informal vote — In some countries, a ballot that doesn't follow the correct rules and so isn't counted
  • Keep it informal — A request to relax, not stand on ceremony
  • On an informal basis — Without official structure or commitment

Words that mean something similar to informal:
Casual, relaxed, unofficial, laid-back, colloquial (for language), everyday, unpretentious, off-the-record, impromptu, friendly

Words that mean the opposite:
Formal, official, ceremonial, structured, rigid, conventional, proper, professional
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
Informal means relaxed, casual, and free from official rules or strict ceremony — the natural, everyday, unstructured side of things, as opposed to the formal, official, and rule-bound side.
8798:
Informality is the quality, character, or state of being relaxed, casual, and free from strict rules, official ceremony, or rigid structure.

To really feel what this word means, you need to understand what it stands against — its opposite, formality. When something is formal, it follows strict rules, rituals, dress codes, and official behavior. When something has informality, all of that is loosened or dropped. The stiffness disappears. The ceremony fades. Things become easy, relaxed, and natural.

Think of informality as the opposite of a rulebook. Where formality says, "Do this, wear that, address people this way, follow this procedure," informality says, "Relax. Be yourself. There's no script here."
What Informality Looks Like in Real Life

Informality doesn't live in just one area of life — it shows up everywhere:

In language and conversation: When people use slang, nicknames, casual phrases like "What's up?" or "No worries," and skip proper titles, their conversation has informality. Contrast that with formal speech: "Good afternoon, Mr. Johnson. I am writing to formally request your assistance." That has very little informality at all.

In events and occasions: A backyard birthday party overflows with informality — guests wander in freely, there's no assigned seating, people talk over each other happily, and no one announces what happens next. A state banquet, on the other hand, is packed with formality — precise seating arrangements, dress codes, rehearsed toasts, and strict order.

In workplaces: A startup where the CEO works alongside interns, everyone uses first names, and meetings happen on bean bags — that's a culture with strong informality. A traditional law firm where junior employees call partners "Sir" or "Ma'am," wear formal suits, and follow rigid hierarchy — that has very little informality.

In written communication: A text to your best friend ("Hey, you free tonight?") has informality. A formal letter to a government office ("Dear Sir or Madam, I respectfully submit this application...") has almost none.

In dress and appearance: Showing up to a casual Sunday brunch in jeans and a T-shirt reflects the informality of the occasion. Wearing the same outfit to a royal wedding would be a serious mismatch with the formality expected there.

One of the most powerful things about informality is the feeling it generates in a room, a conversation, or a relationship. When informality is present, things tend to feel:

  • Warm and friendly — there's closeness between people, not cold distance
  • Relaxed — nobody is on edge worrying about saying or doing the wrong thing
  • Open and approachable — people feel free to speak up, laugh, or share ideas
  • Human — the stiff, official layer is peeled back and people interact as themselves

Informality is often what makes a conversation feel like a real conversation rather than a performance. It's what makes a gathering feel like fun rather than an obligation.
A Critical Distinction: Informality Is Not Rudeness

Many learners confuse informality with being impolite or careless. This is a very important mistake to avoid.

Informality only refers to the absence of rigid rules and ceremony. It says nothing about whether people are kind, respectful, or considerate. You can be completely informal with your close friends — joking, using nicknames, interrupting each other playfully — while still being deeply kind and caring toward them.

Informality is about how loosely structured the interaction is. Rudeness is about how poorly you treat someone. These are two completely separate things.

A doctor who sits casually on the edge of a desk, speaks warmly and uses simple language with a patient, and lets them ask questions freely — that doctor has brought informality to the appointment. That is not rude. In fact, it can be reassuring and compassionate.
When Informality Is a Strength, and When It Becomes a Problem

Informality is not automatically good or bad — what matters is whether it matches the situation.

Informality is a strength when:

  • You're among close friends or family, where it creates natural warmth and closeness.
  • You're in a creative or collaborative environment, where it frees people to take risks and share ideas without fear.
  • You're trying to make someone feel comfortable and at ease.
  • The situation is genuinely casual and calls for a relaxed approach.

Informality becomes a problem when:

  • You use it in a setting that demands ceremony or respect — like being overly casual at a funeral, in a courtroom, or during a formal job interview.
  • You write informal, slangy emails to someone who expects professional communication.
  • You are in a culture where showing respect is done through formality — and your informality reads as disrespect or ignorance of the norms.

The skill in life is learning to read the room — to know when informality is welcomed and when formality is what the situation calls for.

Informality in the singular describes the overall quality or character of something being casual and relaxed:

"The informality of the professor's teaching style made the lectures enjoyable."
"There was a refreshing informality about the way they ran their meetings."

Informalities in the plural refers to specific individual acts or instances of informal behavior:

"The ambassador was surprised by the informalities at the dinner — guests arrived late, called each other by first names, and casually left their seats during the meal."
Common and Natural Ways the Word Is Used

You will often see informality paired with these kinds of phrases:

  • "an atmosphere of informality" — describing the overall relaxed vibe of a place or event
  • "a spirit of informality" — suggesting that casualness was the intention behind something
  • "the informality of the occasion" — noting that the event itself was casual in nature
  • "characteristic informality" — describing someone who is known for being relaxed and casual in their manner
  • "a degree/level of informality" — suggesting that informality exists on a spectrum, and this is how much of it is present
Summary: The Word in One Clear Picture

Imagine two dinner parties. At the first, guests wear elegant clothes, sit in assigned seats, address the host as "Mr." or "Mrs.," follow a formal meal schedule, and speak carefully. At the second, guests show up in whatever they like, sit wherever they want, call the host by a nickname, laugh loudly, and eat whenever the food arrives. The first dinner has formality. The second has informality — it has the quality of being open, unstructured, relaxed, and free from ceremony.

Informality, then, is simply that quality. It is the relaxed, casual, rule-free character that a situation, a relationship, a conversation, an event, or a person's manner can have. It lives at the comfortable, warm, easy end of the spectrum — as far as you can get from stiff ceremonies, strict protocols, and official rules.
8799:
An informant is a person who gives information to someone else — usually to a person or organisation that has a specific reason to want or collect that information. The key idea is that an informant is a source. They know something, and they share it.

That said, the word carries different shades of meaning depending on the situation it is used in. Understanding those situations is what will give you complete mastery of this word.
The Two Main Worlds This Word Lives In

1. The Criminal / Law Enforcement World (Most Common Usage)

This is the sense most people think of first. In this context, an informant is someone who secretly passes information about criminal activity to the police or other authorities.

Think of it this way: imagine a person who is part of a criminal gang, or who simply knows what criminals are doing. Instead of staying quiet, they go to the police and tell them — who is involved, what crimes are being planned, where illegal goods are hidden. That person is an informant.

A few important points about this:

  • Secrecy is central. The informant's identity is usually kept hidden. The criminals being reported on do not know who is talking to the police. This is why authorities often use the phrase confidential informant (often shortened to CI).
  • The motivation varies. An informant might do this out of a sense of justice, but very often there is a personal gain involved — a reduced prison sentence, money, or protection. This is important because it affects how trustworthy the information is considered to be.
  • The relationship is ongoing. An informant is not always someone who just reports one thing. Often, they have a continuing relationship with law enforcement, regularly feeding them information over a period of time.

The detective's most valuable informant had been feeding the department information about the drug ring for over two years.

2. The Academic / Research World

In research — particularly in fields like linguistics, anthropology, and sociology — an informant is someone who provides a researcher with information about their own language, culture, or community.

For example, if a linguist is studying a rare dialect spoken in a small village, they might sit with a local resident and ask them questions: "What do you call this?" "How would you say that?" "What does this word mean to you?" That resident is the linguist's informant. They are the insider source — the person with the lived, authentic knowledge that the researcher needs.

In this context, the word is entirely neutral and carries no negative weight at all. The informant is simply a helpful participant, a knowledgeable insider sharing their expertise.

The anthropologist relied heavily on a local informant to understand the community's traditional rituals.

Note: In modern academic writing, researchers sometimes prefer the word participant or consultant instead of informant in this sense, because of the negative associations the word carries in everyday speech (more on that below). However, informant remains widely used and perfectly correct in academic writing.
The Emotional Weight of the Word — Connotation

This is something a learner absolutely must understand: the word "informant" is not emotionally neutral in everyday life.

When used outside of academic writing, it almost always carries a sense of secrecy, betrayal, or switching sides. An informant is, in some sense, telling on someone — exposing what others wanted kept hidden. Because of this, the word can carry a slightly suspicious or dramatic feeling, even when no crime is involved.

This is why the word is so frequently found in stories about crime, espionage, and corruption. It suggests someone living a double life — appearing loyal to one group while secretly feeding information to another.

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it sits beside its neighbours.

  • Informer — Almost identical in meaning to informant in the criminal sense, but informer feels slightly more old-fashioned and is almost exclusively negative. It strongly implies betrayal. Informant is the more neutral and formal of the two.
  • Snitch — This is the harsh, street-level, insulting version. Calling someone a snitch is deeply derogatory — it means they betrayed their own group by talking to authorities. Never use this in formal writing.
  • Whistleblower — A whistleblower is someone who exposes wrongdoing within an organisation they are part of — like an employee who reveals that their company is breaking the law. The key difference: a whistleblower usually goes public or to regulators, often sacrificing their own career or safety for the public good. The term is generally more heroic in connotation than informant.
  • Source — Used mainly in journalism. A journalist's source is someone who gives them information, often secretly. It is the most neutral of all these words. A source could be an informant, but source has no criminal or betrayal connotation.
  • Mole — A mole is a spy who has been placed inside an organisation specifically to pass secrets out to the enemy. It is more specific than informant and belongs firmly to the world of espionage.

Virtually anyone — but what makes them an informant is the role they play, not who they are. The word describes a function:

  • A criminal who cooperates with police is an informant.
  • A community member who tips off authorities about suspicious activity is an informant.
  • A village elder helping a researcher understand local customs is an informant.
  • An employee who secretly reports their colleagues' misconduct to management could informally be called an informant.

The unifying thread is always the same: they hold information, and they pass it on — usually to someone in a position of authority or with a specific need to know.

ContextWhat the informant doesTone

In law enforcement, an informant secretly gives information about criminals to the police, often for personal benefit. In academia, an informant is a knowledgeable insider who helps a researcher understand a language or culture. In everyday speech, the word carries a feeling of secrecy and, often, betrayal. It is more formal and slightly more neutral than informer or snitch, but less heroic than whistleblower.

The power of the word informant lies in what it implies about access and trust. An informant is not just any observer. They are someone who has been on the inside — trusted by the very group or world they are now reporting on. That is what makes the role so loaded, so valuable to authorities, and so controversial to everyone else. The informant stands at a crossroads between loyalty and disclosure, and that tension is baked into the word itself.
